leads.name: op Romeins fundament
leads.why: Staged 2026-08-22 from Leidschendam-Voorburg, which sits 3.6 km from the The Hague city centre and is inside this site's day-trip boundary, so it belongs on the The Hague page rather than on a thin page of its own. Name the real place honestly in the location fields and the true travel time in transport. LRMB register nr 1686876 ('Plataan op Romeins fundament'). Register planting band 1700-1750, so the age is a BAND and must not be sharpened. Register records it as publicly visitable; owner category gemeente, setting park. Register history of the PLACE, not of the tree, so do not bridge from it: De plataan in park Hoekenburg staat op historische grond; de geschiedenis van de omgeving gaat terug tot ver voor het begin van onze jaartelling. De Romeinen vestigden de havenstad Forum Hadrianum op de plek van een eerdere nederzetting van de Kaninefaten, de oorspronkelijke bewoners van ons land. Oude resten van de Romeinse stad zijn in 2008 gevonden in de omgeving. Ook de resten van een paal zijn toen blootgelegd, gemaakt uit hout van een in 212 gekapte eik (jaarringenonderzoek). De plataan staat letterlijk op de plaats waar de geschiedenis van Voorburg is begonnen. De boom is in zijn 300 jarig bestaan uitgegroeid tot een icoon van de omgeving: bij renovatie van het park is de boom goed beschermd. Het is de dikste plataan van Zuid-Holland. The register is ONE source. A second is wanted; without one the tree still ships with curation_status flagged.

leads.name: The Juttepeer of Heilige Geesthofje
leads.why: PULLED FROM THE LIVE PAGE 2026-08-29 on hard rule 10. Guided Buitenmuseum tours by appointment, or one open-monuments day a year, and the access line said in so many words that it is not open to casual walk-in visitors. An annual open day is not open access. Nothing is wrong with the tree and the research is kept here in full; it can go back the day the access changes. Access as published: Restricted: guided Buitenmuseum tours, by appointment, or during Open Monumentendag. Not open to casual walk-in visitors
leads.story: Elderly women living in this almshouse have been making jelly from this pear tree's fruit since at least the 17th century, and the tree they are picking from is very likely the same one their predecessors used four centuries ago. Planted in 1638 in the inner courtyard of the Heilige Geesthofje, founded in 1616 to house women of unblemished character, the tree is widely considered the oldest pear tree in the Netherlands, a juttepeer, a small, hard, old Dutch variety better suited to cooking and preserving than eating straight off the branch. The courtyard itself functioned as a working kitchen garden for residents for most of its history, vegetables and fruit grown for the household rather than for show, and the pear outlasted whatever else was once planted alongside it. It still bears fruit every year, harvested and turned into jelly by the almshouse's current residents in a tradition nobody has needed to formally revive because it never actually stopped. The courtyard is not casually open to passersby; the almshouse still functions as a residence, and visiting means booking a guided tour through the Buitenmuseum, arranging an appointment, or timing a visit to the national Open Monumentendag, a small price for standing beside something planted six years before Rembrandt painted the Night Watch.

leads.name: The Bezuidenhoutseweg Oak
leads.age_estimate: 225 to 275 years, planted somewhere between 1750 and 1800

location.address: Koekamp, beside the Bezuidenhoutseweg, Den Haag

leads.story: Four minutes north of the platforms at Den Haag Centraal, on the old deer meadow called the Koekamp, stands an oak the national register dates to somewhere between 1750 and 1800. That is a fifty year shrug rather than a date, and it still makes the tree at least 225 years old, possibly closer to 275. The Koekamp is why it is here. This strip beside the Haagse Bos has been grazing meadow for centuries, cattle first and deer later, land that was never built on and never laid out as a garden, so the trees on it were left to get old rather than pruned into a design. Not all of them got the chance. During the German occupation a great many trees around the Koekamp went into stoves as firewood or were cut down to clear the line of a tank ditch dug across this side of the city. This oak stayed standing through both. It has no name, no plaque and no recorded history, it belongs to the state forestry service, and it is one of the easiest old trees in the Netherlands to reach: out of the station, over the road, and there it is. If you know who planted it, we would like to hear.
verified_sources: Landelijk Register Monumentale Bomen v2024 (Bomenstichting), register nr 1686943: Zomereik, Koekamp, Naast Internationaal Water House Bezuidenhoutseweg, Den Haag, planting band 1750-1800, reason for protection 'monumentaal', owner staatsbosbeheer, recorded as visitable
Bomenstichting Den Haag, 2026-08-18: the local branch pointed us at the national register as the source for The Hague's monumental trees; register data used with written permission.
leads.access: Free, open parkland on the Koekamp, at any time
leads.transport: Four minute walk north from Den Haag Centraal

best_time.label: September to October: acorns drop, and a good mast year buries the ground in them

leads.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it as the unmarked oak with no plaque, standing alone on the old deer meadow. It stands on the Koekamp beside the Bezuidenhoutseweg, four minutes' walk from Den Haag Centraal.

leads.name: The Grandbos Beech

location.address: Le Grandbos, Van Soutelandelaan at Van Mojalenlaan, Mariahoeve, Den Haag

leads.story: Nothing about the corner of the Van Soutelandelaan and the Van Mojalenlaan announces a two hundred year old tree. The beech stands in a strip of wood called Le Grandbos, a leftover of the estate landscape that was here before Mariahoeve was built over it, and the register dates the tree to the 1820s. Beech does two things worth the walk. Its bark stays smooth and grey for its whole life, so an old trunk reads more like a column than a tree, without the deep furrows that give an oak of the same age away. And it holds autumn better than almost anything else growing in a Dutch street, going copper in late October and keeping it into November, with the fallen leaves staying orange on the ground for weeks afterwards. Underneath it, very little grows. A mature beech takes so much of the light that the ground under the crown stays bare, which is the easiest way to pick one out of a mixed wood from a distance. An oak of nearly the same vintage stands about two hundred metres off, on the other side of the Van Soutelandelaan, so this is a ten minute detour with two trees in it.

best_time.label: late October into November, when the beech turns copper and keeps it for weeks

Bomenstichting Den Haag, 2026-08-18: the local branch pointed us at the national register as the source for The Hague's monumental trees; register data used with written permission.

leads.name: The Malieveld Elm
leads.story: An elm from the 1830s has outlived two epidemics that killed almost everything of its kind. Dutch elm disease takes its name from the country that first identified it, in the years after the First World War, and a second, far more aggressive strain arrived in the 1970s and finished most of what the first had left. Between them they emptied Dutch streets of the tree that had defined them for centuries. This one went into the ground somewhere between 1830 and 1840 and is still standing, on the field where the country goes to be heard. The Malieveld began as a court for pall mall, the ball and mallet game the 17th century was mad about, and became the open ground in the middle of The Hague where farmers park their tractors, unions bring their whistles and hundreds of thousands of people have gathered for one cause or another. Between demonstrations it takes funfairs and circus tents. The elm has stood at the edge of all of it for close to two centuries, a short walk from the parliament buildings everybody comes here to shout at, and almost nobody in those crowds has ever looked up at it.
verified_sources: Landelijk Register Monumentale Bomen v2024 (Bomenstichting), register nr 1686946: Monumentaaliep, Malieveld, Den Haag, planting band 1830-1840, reason for protection 'monumentaal', owner gemeente, recorded as visitable; the register's Dutch name 'Monumentaaliep' points at the 'Monumentalis' selection of Ulmus x hollandica, so we record the species at the level we can defend
Bomenstichting Den Haag, 2026-08-18: the local branch pointed us at the national register as the source for The Hague's monumental trees; register data used with written permission.
leads.access: Free, the open Malieveld, at any time
leads.transport: Ten minute walk from Den Haag Centraal
leads.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it as the old elm standing at the edge of the open Malieveld, near the parliament buildings. It stands alone at the field's border, close to where demonstrations and funfairs gather.

blocked.name: The Copper Beech South of the Vreugd en Rust Koepel
blocked.age_estimate: roughly 190 years, from a registered planting date around 1840

location.address: Zuidkant Koepel nr 1, Park Vreugd en Rust, Voorburg

blocked.story:
Nearly all of a mature beech's roots sit in the top half metre of soil, spread about as wide as the crown reaches. Stand under this one and you are standing on it. That shallow plate is why old beeches in well used parks tend to die of nothing more dramatic than feet: the ground packs down, air stops reaching the roots, and a tree that has held on for nearly two centuries loses to a shortcut worn across the grass. Anyone looking after a park beech worries about the soil long before the branches.

This is the southern of the two copper beeches at koepel number one in Park Vreugd en Rust. The national register gives it a planting date somewhere between 1830 and 1840, so roughly 190 years, and that band is an estimate of when it went in rather than a count of rings. The register is the only source that puts any number on it.

Come in a mast year and you will hear the tree before you look at it. Beech drops its nuts in irregular gluts rather than evenly, and after a heavy one the spiky husks lie thick enough underfoot to crunch. The park is in Voorburg, part of Leidschendam-Voorburg, a short ride east of The Hague rather than a walk within it.
blocked.transport: Voorburg railway station, a few minutes by train from Den Haag Centraal, then about an 8-minute walk.
blocked.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it as the southern of two copper beeches standing together at koepel number one. It stands in Park Vreugd en Rust, Voorburg.
blocked.removed_reason: Dead: LRMB status 5 (dood/geveld). hag_026 Vreugd en Rust copper beech cut back in 2014, only a memorial trunk left; hag_031 Juliana en Bernardpark beech, last seen May 2020. Retired 2026-10-12 on Hidde's word.

blocked.name: The Stone Bench Beech of Juliana en Bernardpark
blocked.age_estimate: roughly 160 years, from a registered planting date around 1870
blocked.story:
A beech that grows alone is a different shape of tree from a beech that grows in a wood. In a forest it races its neighbours upward and ends as a long clean column with the crown somewhere overhead. Given open ground it keeps its low limbs, spreads sideways and often finishes wider than it is tall. This one has had open ground in the Juliana en Bernardpark for about 160 years, and the outline shows which life it got.

The national register puts the planting between 1860 and 1870 and locates the tree by the stone bench rather than by any house number, which is still the best direction anyone can give. So: roughly 160 years, from an estimate of the planting rather than a count of rings. Nobody has cored it, and the register is the only source that dates it at all.

That span covers the turning of Voorburg from a village of country estates into a suburb of The Hague, and the occupation, and every winter storm in between. None of it shows on the tree. Beech holds smooth grey bark to the end, which is why the only honest measure of one is its girth.

Voorburg belongs to the municipality of Leidschendam-Voorburg, east of The Hague and outside the city, so this is a ride out rather than a stroll.
blocked.transport: Voorburg railway station, a few minutes by train from Den Haag Centraal, then about a 10-minute walk.

best_time.label: October to November: copper and russet, and young trees keep dead leaves all winter

blocked.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by its wide, low, spreading shape, a beech that grew alone rather than crowded by a wood. It stands by the stone bench in Juliana en Bernardpark, Voorburg.
blocked.removed_reason: Dead: LRMB status 5 (dood/geveld). hag_026 Vreugd en Rust copper beech cut back in 2014, only a memorial trunk left; hag_031 Juliana en Bernardpark beech, last seen May 2020. Retired 2026-10-12 on Hidde's word.

notes.what: Its approximate pin (52.0838873,4.3225274) sits beside the register's 'Zomereiken Hertenkamp', a group of SEVENTEEN oaks planted 1700-1750, which also matches our stated age of about 300 years. hag_006, added the same day, is the register's separate SINGLE oak 193 m east at the Bezuidenhoutseweg end, band 1750-1800. So they are two different trees and were correctly written as two.
